overview:
Interlinear commentary is a method of scriptural explanation in which brief glosses, synonyms, grammatical cues, or paraphrases are written directly between the lines or in very close proximity to the base text, often in a smaller script. In Jain traditions, this practice developed as a way to make dense Prakrit or Sanskrit canonical and philosophical texts accessible to students, monks, and lay scholars who needed help with language, grammar, and doctrinal nuance.

Unlike separate, running commentaries (ṭīkā, vṛtti, or bhāṣya) that expand on a passage in continuous prose, interlinear commentary typically stays close to the word order of the root text. Each term or phrase may be followed by a synonym, a short explanation, or a grammatical identification. This allows the reader to see the original wording and its interpretive aid at the same time, preserving the authority of the root text while guiding understanding. In many Jain manuscripts, the root text is written in a larger script, with the interlinear gloss in smaller letters inserted above, below, or between the lines.

Historically, interlinear commentary has been important in the transmission of Jain canonical texts (āgama) and philosophical works such as the Tattvārthasūtra. As Jain communities moved across regions and languages, interlinear glosses helped bridge Prakrit or Sanskrit originals with local vernaculars, and they also recorded how particular lineages understood key doctrinal terms. For example, technical vocabulary about karma, guṇasthāna (spiritual stages), or vows might be clarified with concise definitions or doctrinal cross-references written right next to the sutra.

From a pedagogical perspective, interlinear commentary supports memorization and recitation. Students can chant the root text while glancing at the glosses to recall meaning. In some educational settings, teachers use interlinear notes as a scaffold, later encouraging advanced students to rely more directly on the root text. At the same time, interlinear commentary can reveal layers of interpretation: different manuscripts may preserve slightly different glosses, showing how doctrinal emphasis or linguistic understanding shifted over time.

In modern Jain studies, interlinear commentary is also significant for textual criticism and history. Scholars examine how glosses relate to larger, independent commentaries, how they reflect sectarian perspectives (Digambara, Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, Terāpanth), and how they interact with evolving vernaculars such as Gujarati, Hindi, or Kannada. Careful attention is needed to distinguish the original canonical or philosophical text from later interlinear additions, especially when preparing critical editions or translations. Thus, interlinear commentary is both a practical teaching tool and a valuable historical record of how Jain texts have been understood and transmitted across centuries.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra (example of a sutra often accompanied by interlinear glosses in manuscripts)
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi (traditionally attributed)
primary_sources.translation: Right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct constitute the path to liberation.
primary_sources.notes: In many Jain manuscript traditions, this foundational sutra is written in a larger script, while brief interlinear glosses explain each term: ‘samyag-darśana’ may be glossed as ‘niścaya-sraddhā’ (true conviction), ‘jñāna’ as ‘tattva-jñāna’ (knowledge of realities), and ‘cāritra’ as ‘saṃyama’ (self-restraint in conduct). These glosses can appear between lines or above the words, providing immediate doctrinal and linguistic clarification without forming a separate running commentary. Later, more extensive works such as Pūjyapāda’s Sarvārthasiddhi offer a full prose commentary, but the interlinear notes in manuscripts show how teachers and scribes guided readers at the level of individual words and phrases.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayanasūtra (illustrative of canonical verses with interlinear vernacular glosses)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to early Jain teachers; preserved in Śvetāmbara canon
primary_sources.original_text: णं च णं च विणा लोए, णं च णं च विणा दव्वे।
primary_sources.transliteration: ṇaṃ ca ṇaṃ ca viṇā loe, ṇaṃ ca ṇaṃ ca viṇā davve.
primary_sources.translation: There is no (true) world without the soul, and there is no (true) substance without the soul.
primary_sources.notes: In Śvetāmbara manuscript and teaching traditions, verses from the Uttarādhyayanasūtra are often accompanied by interlinear glosses in Gujarati or Hindi that clarify Prakrit vocabulary and doctrinal implications. For example, ‘loea’ (world) may be glossed as ‘saṃsāra’ (cycle of rebirth), and ‘davve’ (substance) as ‘dravya’ with a short note on the six fundamental substances. These glosses are written between or above the lines of the Prakrit text, helping students who are less familiar with Prakrit to understand the canonical verse while still seeing the original wording.

misconceptions.myth: Interlinear commentary is the same as a full, independent commentary and can be treated as part of the original scripture.
misconceptions.reality: Interlinear commentary is typically a later pedagogical or explanatory layer added around a root text. It is not identical to a full prose commentary (ṭīkā or bhāṣya), and it should not be confused with the original canonical or philosophical composition. When studying or editing Jain texts, it is important to distinguish the base text from interlinear glosses and to recognize that these glosses reflect particular historical and sectarian perspectives.

misconceptions.myth: Interlinear commentary is only a mechanical word-for-word translation and has no doctrinal significance.
misconceptions.reality: While many interlinear glosses are brief and focus on synonyms or grammar, they often carry doctrinal choices—selecting one meaning over another, highlighting certain aspects of karma, vows, or metaphysics, or aligning a term with a specific sectarian interpretation. As a result, interlinear commentary can be an important witness to how different Jain communities understood and taught the same root text, and it deserves careful attention in both traditional study and modern scholarship.
